subject: [RFC PATCH 0/5] mm: sub-folio dirty tracking for PTE-mapped mmap writes

reviews.author: Pedro Falcato
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Pedro Falcato expressed uncertainty about the current state of a related patch series by Willy, but did not provide any specific technical feedback or concerns regarding the submitted patch.

Reviewer Pedro Falcato questioned the assumption that page_mkwrite is not always called, pointing out that it is indeed invoked in do_shared_fault(), and requested clarification on when the described scenario occurs.

Reviewer Pedro Falcato expressed concern that the patch introduces multiple methods for dirtying folios, contradicting the goal of having a single method.

Reviewer Pedro Falcato noted that sub-folio dirty tracking does not make sense because the whole folio is still dirty, and requested additional logic to handle split file folios for reclaim purposes.
reviews.raw_body:
Hmm, I believe Willy already had some patches; I don't know what came of
them (I think he's out for now).

---

Help me out here: in which case does this happen? page fault handling is a
mess... I think page_mkwrite is always called, no? in do_shared_fault().

---

I think this goes against what we're trying to pull off. We want a single
method of dirtying folios, not 3.

Ideally(tm) we would have a single mkwrite interface.

---

That is correct; I don't think doing subpage accounting makes any sense,
the whole folio is still dirty, and for reclaim purposes can't be thrown
away (unless you added gnarly split logic for file folios as well).

reviews.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
reviews.summary: The author addressed a concern about the frequency of folio_mkclean() calls, explaining that it is always called once per folio, not once per page, and that mapping the entire folio is necessary to accurately count mlocked memory. The author confirmed that narrowing the dirtying to a subset of pages is not possible once the whole folio is mapped.
reviews.raw_body:
It is always called, but once per folio, not once per page. It is the
filesystem's chance to preallocate whatever it needs to track dirty
state for the *folio*.

Later finish_fault() maps the folio. It tries to map it fully when it
can, so a write fault creates up to 512 writable PTEs on x86. And we
really do need to map the folio fully whenever we can. Otherwise we
significantly undercount mlocked memory. See commit 19773df031bc
("mm/fault: try to map the entire file folio in finish_fault()").

And once the whole folio is mapped with writable PTEs we cannot narrow
the dirtying to a subset of pages. Any of them can turn dirty at any
time, with nothing to record it.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

2026-09-03.patch_summary: This patch set introduces sub-folio dirty tracking for PTE-mapped mmap writes, addressing the issue of large page cache folios being dirtied unnecessarily when a single byte is written through a shared file mapping. The problem arises because current implementations mark the entire folio as dirty, leading to inefficient writeback and increased minor fault counts. To solve this, the patch harvests hardware PTE dirty bits at page_mkwrite() time and provides the filesystem with the ranges that were actually modified, allowing for more targeted writeback. This approach is already implemented in XFS and is shown to reduce writeback by 99% on a large file system.

reviews.author: Kiryl Shutsemau
reviews.summary: Reviewer Kiryl Shutsemau agrees to remove the ->dirty_folio() function, which makes little sense, and instead proposes bundling dirtying into ->page_mkwrite(). He suggests that this distinction between making a folio writable and marking it dirty is meaningful, allowing filesystems to provide fine-grained dirty tracking through ->dirty_folio_range().
reviews.raw_body:
Boris pointed me to Matthew's proposal to remove ->dirty_folio:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/aoyWln-Gt-yvZQkE@casper.infradead.org

I agree that the current ->dirty_folio() makes little sense and that
dirtying the folio can be bundled into ->page_mkwrite(), as they are
matched 1-to-1.

My proposal makes the distinction between making the folio writable and
making it dirty meaningful. ->page_mkwrite() allocates whatever is needed
on the filesystem side to track dirty state and drive writeback for the
*folio*, while ->dirty_folio_range() marks part of the folio dirty.

We can still drop ->dirty_folio(). A filesystem can provide
->dirty_folio_range() if it wants fine-grained (sub-folio) dirty
tracking.

A separate question is whether we want to avoid installing a writable PMD
entry for filesystems that want fine-grained dirty tracking. I have a
patch for this, but it deserves a separate discussion once we agree that we
want this for PTE-mapped folios first.

Any feedback?

reviews.author: Usama Arif
reviews.summary: Reviewer noted that holding the page-table lock does not prevent the CPU from setting the hardware dirty bit, creating a timing window where the bitmap is populated from an outdated snapshot of PTEs and the final dirty state correctness-critical.
reviews.raw_body:
The patch reads the PTE first and then records pte_dirty(entry) in the bitmap
before invalidating the PTE.

Holding the page-table lock prevents another kernel thread from changing
the PTE, but it does not prevent the CPU from setting the hardware dirty
bit.

This sequence is possible:

  Writeback CPU                  Application CPU
  -------------                  ---------------
  ptep_get(): writable, clean
                                 store through the PTE
                                 hardware sets dirty
  ptep_clear_flush(): returns dirty PTE
  pte_mkclean()
  reinstall clean, read-only PTE

The bitmap was populated from the first, clean snapshot. The dirty state
returned by ptep_clear_flush() is discarded.

With range-aware iomap writeback:

- The folio can still be selected for writeback.
- The affected filesystem block is absent from the iomap dirty bitmap.
- Writeback clears the folio dirty state without writing that block.
- Later eviction can discard the modified data.

The old whole-folio behavior did not need to know which PTE became
dirty, so this timing window was harmless. Sub-folio tracking makes the
final dirty state correctness-critical.

The PMD path has the identical race between pmdp_get() and
pmdp_invalidate().

reviews.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
reviews.summary: Author responded to a question about the generality of the math presented in the patch, stating that it applies equally to any architecture with 2M THP/mTHP and 4k PAGE_SIZE.
reviews.raw_body:
No, that was x86. But the math is the same on any arch with 2M THP/mTHP
in page cache and 4k PAGE_SIZE.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

reviews.author: Usama Arif
reviews.summary: Reviewer Usama Arif noted that folio_mark_dirty() clears the PG_reclaim flag, but mapping_dirty_range() does not, and asked if it is necessary to clear PG_reclaim in this case
reviews.raw_body:
folio_mark_dirty() clears PG_reclaim, but mapping_dirty_range() doesnt.
Do you need to clear PG_reclaim here?
